description: Descriptions of standardized NDIS INF keywords shown by the adapter inspector. Vendor keywords without an asterisk are shown with the driver's own display name.

keywords.description: Link speed and duplex. Auto negotiation is right for almost every network; forcing a speed can cause duplex mismatches.
Ethernet pause frames that let a busy device ask the other side to wait. Usually left at the driver default.
Maximum frame size. Jumbo frames only help on networks where every device supports them; leave at 1514 for internet gaming.
Batches interrupts to lower CPU load. Turning it off can lower latency slightly at the cost of more interrupts (catalog item net.interrupt-moderation-off).
Inserts 802.1p priority and VLAN tags. Needed for QoS tagging on some networks.
Receive side scaling: spreads receive processing across several cores (catalog item net.rss-on).
How RSS picks processors (for example NUMA static or closest).
Number of receive queues RSS may use.
First logical processor RSS may use. A base above 0 keeps receive processing off core 0.
Maximum number of processors RSS may use.
Highest logical processor RSS may use.
Receive descriptors. More buffers absorb bursts (fewer discarded packets) and use a little more memory.
Transmit descriptors. Rarely needs changing.
Lets the adapter compute IPv4 header checksums instead of the CPU.
Lets the adapter compute TCP checksums over IPv4.
Lets the adapter compute TCP checksums over IPv6.
Lets the adapter compute UDP checksums over IPv4 (most game traffic is UDP).
Lets the adapter compute UDP checksums over IPv6.
Large send offload for IPv4: the adapter splits large TCP sends into packets. Helps throughput, not game latency.
Large send offload for IPv6.
Receive segment coalescing for IPv4: merges received TCP segments to save CPU. Does not apply to UDP game traffic.
Receive segment coalescing for IPv6.
Virtual machine queues for Hyper-V virtual switches. Not used without Hyper-V networking.
Single root I/O virtualization for virtual machines. Not used on a typical gaming PC.
Wake the PC from sleep when a magic packet arrives (Wake-on-LAN).
Wake the PC on network traffic patterns. Can cause unexpected wake-ups.
Answers ARP requests while the PC sleeps, so it stays reachable without waking.
Answers IPv6 neighbor solicitations while the PC sleeps.
Wake-on-LAN magic packets during Modern Standby.
Lets the adapter enter a low-power state when idle (USB and some PCIe adapters).
Holds some broadcast and multicast packets to save power; can add latency to such packets.
Overrides the adapter's MAC address.
